title: Babel's Tower and Abram's Family
overview: People try to build a city and tower so they can stay together and make a name for themselves, God scatters them by confusing their language, and the story then narrows to the family of Abram.

parts.label: One people, one plan (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: In Shinar, the river plain of southern Iraq, people build with baked brick and tar, the usual materials there, and many scholars link the tower to the stepped temple towers of ancient Babylon. The text never names their wrong outright, but many readers see pride in wanting "a name" and resistance to God's earlier call to fill the earth (9:1).

parts.label: The LORD comes down (vv. 5-7)
parts.note: Many readers notice the irony that a tower meant to reach heaven is so small the LORD must come down to see it, and God judges that a united humanity could do whatever it set out to do (v. 6). God's "let us" (v. 7) may be spoken to a heavenly court, as many Jewish readers and scholars hold, or may hint at God as Trinity, as many Christians have traditionally read it.

parts.label: Scattered at Babel (vv. 8-9)
parts.note: Unable to understand each other, the people stop building and spread out, and the place is called Babel, the Hebrew name for Babylon, which sounds like the Hebrew word for "confuse." Christians often read Acts 2, where people of many languages each hear one message in their own tongue, as a reversal of Babel.

parts.label: From Shem to Abram (vv. 10-26)
parts.note: Ten generations run from Shem to Abram, matching the ten from Adam to Noah in chapter 5, and lifespans shrink overall from Shem's 600 years, though not evenly (Eber outlives both his father and grandfather). Whether the ages are meant literally is debated, and the ancient Greek translation gives different numbers and adds one extra name.

parts.label: Terah's family in Ur (vv. 27-30)
parts.note: Terah's son Haran dies in Ur before his father, and Haran's brother Nahor marries Haran's daughter Milkah, an uncle and niece marriage the text reports without comment. The flat statement that Sarai cannot have children (v. 30) sets up the central tension of Abram's story to come.

parts.label: Stopping at Harran (vv. 31-32)
parts.note: Terah sets out for Canaan but settles at Harran, a city far to the north in today's southeastern Turkey, and dies there. Joshua 24:2 later says Terah worshiped other gods, and the next chapter opens with God calling Abram to go on.

disagreement: Christians differ on what Babel mainly shows: many see human pride and defiance of God being judged, while others read the scattering and new languages as God's gift of diversity and a check on any drive toward one controlling empire.
think: When does the urge to stay together and make a name for ourselves bring out the best in people, and when does it start to do harm?
